name: Lifetime
label: Jade Tree
lede: Dan Yemin moved from Michigan to New Jersey in 1989 to start a band. Two Jade Tree records and about 45 minutes later, Lifetime was done, and the next decade's emo bands were covering the songs.

eras.title: A Michigan kid comes east to start a band
eras.text: Dan Yemin crossed from Michigan to New Jersey with one goal and found a singer in Ari Katz, late of the local band Enuf. That first Lifetime was a scrappy New Brunswick hardcore band, and it left one LP, Background, on New Age Records.

years.h: Dan Yemin leaves Michigan for New Jersey with one plan
years.p: Yemin later told Punknews the ambition was small: make something somebody liked enough to put out a 7-inch.

years.h: Ari Katz and Dan Yemin start Lifetime in New Brunswick
years.p: Katz arrives from the local band Enuf. Yemin says the name comes from the second [[Rollins Band|3ca37f23-fdce-49ce-86e2-134c9a17ebc5]] album, Lifetime; Katz says it doesn't.
years.xp:
Asked about the name sixteen years later, Yemin credited the Rollins Band record. Katz remembers it differently, and Yemin told Punknews: "Ari claims that's not where we got it from, so I dunno. We remember it differently."

What they agreed on was the lyrical line. Katz steered away from the tough-guy violence of New York hardcore toward what Wikipedia calls positive, personal themes, which became the band's signature.

years.h: A first West Coast trip turns up two friends for life
years.p: Two women Dan Yemin met at the July or August 1991 California shows stayed friends with the band and turned up at its 2005 reunion shows.

years.h: Background gets tracked at SRA Music Studio in Scotch Plains
years.p: The first line-up is Katz, Yemin, guitarist Scott Saint Hilaire, bassist Justin Janisch and drummer David Wagenschutz. Bonus live tracks come from Lost Horizons in Syracuse, July 5, 1992.

years.src: Wikipedia: Background · Punknews · Lifetime on Bandcamp
years.h: Background comes out as New Age Records No. 15
years.p: The California straight-edge label puts out the debut LP. Break Even Point presses 1,000 copies of a European edition retitled Ghost.
years.xp:
Nobody in the band got sentimental about it. When fans asked for Background songs at the reunion, Yemin's reply to Punknews was "Do you have ears?"

Bassist Dave Palaitis later remixed the whole album for the 2006 Jade Tree set Somewhere in the Swamps of New Jersey, which pairs his remix with the original.

eras.title: A new line-up and a young label in Delaware
eras.text: With a rebuilt five-piece and producer Steve Evetts, Lifetime cut two short, fast, hooky records for Jade Tree. Hello Bastards and Jersey's Best Dancers set love songs and Hüsker Dü melody inside hardcore, and the band broke up right after the second.

years.cap: Ari Katz singing with Dave Palaitis on bass, Santa Barbara
years.h: Pete Martin, Dave Palaitis and Scott Golley fill out the band
years.p: Guitarist Martin, bassist Palaitis and drummer Golley are the five-piece that plays on both Jade Tree albums.

years.h: Steve Evetts takes the board for Hello Bastards
years.p: Evetts produces and engineers at Trax East in South River, New Jersey, in May and June 1995. The studio keeps coming back into this story with [[Kid Dynamite|c5300096-cfb0-4801-b146-166e2d02f08a]].

years.src: Wikipedia: Hello Bastards · Lifetime on Bandcamp
years.h: Hello Bastards is over in 21 minutes and 37 seconds
years.p: Twelve songs on Jade Tree, one of them a cover of [[Hüsker Dü|5c4c90a4-539f-4101-83cf-301bc6a94e06]]'s It's Not Funny Anymore. The play track, Daneurysm, opens the record.
years.xp:
Wikipedia lists the release as September 25, 1995; Lifetime's own Bandcamp says September 1. Either way it was early Jade Tree, a label run out of Wilmington, Delaware.

Wikipedia notes that Vulture later ranked (The Gym Is) Neutral Territory No. 52 on its list of the 100 best emo songs. AllMusic and Punknews each gave the album 3.5 stars.

years.h: Glue Records gathers the 7-inches and the leftovers
years.p: The compilation of singles and unreleased songs comes out on Glue Records in the US and Day After Records in Europe.

years.h: Back to South River for the next record
years.p: Steve Evetts tracks Jersey's Best Dancers at Trax East in two bursts, June 1996 and January 1997.

years.cap: Flyer for Lifetime, Garden Variety, Weston, Plow and Trusty, Wetlands, New York, Feb. 25
years.src: Wikipedia: Jersey's Best Dancers · Wikipedia: Lifetime (band)
years.h: Jersey's Best Dancers, then everyone covers it
years.p: Twenty-three minutes, and Pitchfork gave it 8.5. [[Fall Out Boy|516cef4d-0718-4007-9939-f9b38af3f784]] took Turnpike Gates, [[New Found Glory|6acb932e-840d-47ac-8e0d-725ad8a6e52c]] Cut the Tension and [[Rise Against|606bf117-494f-4864-891f-09d63ff6aa4b]] The Boy's No Good.
years.xp:
AllMusic called it a triumphant burst of upbeat punk rock and said the band "called it quits while they were still at the top of their game." AbsolutePunk gave it 91%, and it turned up on best-of lists from Kerrang!, Rock Sound and Rolling Stone.

The bands that name Lifetime as a root read like the next decade's Warped Tour bill: My Chemical Romance, Thursday, Saves the Day, Taking Back Sunday, Midtown and Senses Fail among them.

years.big: Some people in the band didn't want to tour anymore
yt: Final show at the Melody, New Brunswick, Nov. 22, 1997
years.h: Lifetime breaks up after a short tour for Jersey's Best Dancers
years.p: Dan Yemin told Punknews the band divided into two camps over a major touring commitment.
years.xp: Yemin put it to Punknews as a choice between doing it or not doing it at all, with some members out on touring. He also admitted the band had drifted from the fun of it: "We were worrying too much about what other people thought."

years.cap: Dan Yemin with a mohawk, Denver
years.h: Yemin takes the speed to Philadelphia as Kid Dynamite
years.p: With former Lifetime drummer Dave Wagenschutz, he starts [[Kid Dynamite|c5300096-cfb0-4801-b146-166e2d02f08a]], a Philly band built on the same speed and melody.

eras.title: Hellfest dies, Lifetime doesn't
eras.text: A festival reunion collapsed at the last minute, so the band booked its own shows and liked it enough to stay. Within a year Lifetime had a reissue on Jade Tree and a deal with Pete Wentz's label.

years.cap: Ari Katz sings to a packed floor at a Lifetime show
years.h: Hellfest falls apart, so Lifetime books three shows of its own
years.p: The band was due at Hellfest on August 20, 2005. When it collapsed, Lifetime played the Trocadero in Philadelphia, the Starlight Ballroom, and the Stone Pony in Asbury Park with [[The Bouncing Souls|429d5f26-329c-41cc-bdff-17c29dbf1fb8]].
years.xp:
The Trocadero night on August 19 also brought back [[108|7f0c252a-bd45-4fe0-b306-478eeb07b97b]]. The Stone Pony show on August 21 added The Loved Ones, and its profits went to New Labor, The OUT Fund, the Nature Conservancy and Linda Ann's Greyhound Rescue.

Yemin told Punknews a Philadelphia show sold out a 1,200-person room online in about four minutes, and that Lifetime keeps no barricade: if kids get on stage, it's a party.

years.h: Lifetime says it's back for good
years.p: The November 17, 2005 statement rules out a one-off comeback.
years.xp: The band said it would continue "not as the resurrected corpse of a one-off reunion show, but as a group of guys who love making music together."

years.h: The reunion reaches Los Angeles, Anaheim and San Francisco
years.p: Three nights, January 27 to 29, at the Troubadour, Chain Reaction and Slim's, fifteen years after the band's first California trip.

years.h: A free show at SXSW in Austin
years.p: Donations from the March 17 set go to breast cancer research through Shirts for a Cure.

years.h: Jade Tree digs up the singles, demos and covers
years.p: Somewhere in the Swamps of New Jersey is a double disc that includes Background twice, as Dave Palaitis's remix and as the original. The book runs 52 pages with 40-plus rare photos.

years.cap: Lifetime at the Court Tavern, New Brunswick, May 6, 2006
years.h: Pete Wentz signs Lifetime to Decaydance
years.p: The band lands on the Fueled by Ramen imprint run by [[Fall Out Boy|516cef4d-0718-4007-9939-f9b38af3f784]]'s [[Pete Wentz|26cea341-dfab-483f-9cdb-8de82da81019]], one of the kids its records had raised.
years.xp:
Wentz said he signed them "because the world needs another Lifetime record."

The band's own pitch was control: Decaydance would let them make the record they wanted "while still staying in control of our music."

eras.title: One more album, then no label
eras.text: Lifetime made its first album in ten years with the same producer in the same studio, then walked away from Fueled by Ramen. The members kept busy in other bands while the old records got reissued and covered.

years.cap: Lifetime at The Axis, Boston, Feb. 11, 2007
years.h: The self-titled Lifetime lands ten years after the last one
years.p: Recorded in fall 2006 at Trax East with Steve Evetts and done in 21:30. Punknews named it the No. 2 release of 2007; Pitchfork gave it 7.9.
years.xp: AllMusic gave it four stars and said "the guys may be older and more mature" but were still the same hardcore kids at heart. AbsolutePunk gave it 86%.

years.h: Lifetime walks away from Fueled by Ramen
years.p: Punknews reported the split in January 2009, less than two years after the self-titled album, and the band became free agents.

years.h: Two August dates opening for the Bouncing Souls
years.p: Lifetime supports fellow New Jersey lifers [[The Bouncing Souls|429d5f26-329c-41cc-bdff-17c29dbf1fb8]] for two shows in August 2009.

years.h: No Idea reissues Hello Bastards on colored vinyl
years.p: On February 20, 2010 the Gainesville label presses the 12-inch in white, purple and green.

years.h: After 14 years, Lifetime says it's writing again
years.p: Brooklyn Vegan picked up the band's Facebook update in May 2021. Members had spent the gap in [[Paint It Black|90910a44-7579-4730-9499-0546159fe4e3]], Beach Rats and Open City.
